output.impression: Multi-domain cognitive impairment with amnestic predominance, at a level consistent with mild dementia given the reported functional decline. Verbal episodic memory is severely impaired (RAVLT immediate recall 3rd percentile, delayed recall 1st percentile) and recognition does not compensate (4th percentile), consistent with a storage-type deficit. Visual memory is also impaired (Rey Complex Figure delayed recall 5th percentile) despite preserved copy (25th percentile). Semantic fluency (Animals, 8th percentile) and confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 18th percentile) are below expected norms; letter fluency (FAS, 22nd percentile) and set-shifting (Trail Making B, 15th percentile) are mildly reduced. Processing speed (Trail Making A, 28th percentile) is low-normal. Mood screen normal (GDS 3/15). Screening scores: MMSE 21/30, MoCA 17/30.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure 15 cmH2O. Acellular CSF (WBC 2 cells/uL, no red cells) with normal protein (45.6 mg/dL) and glucose (72.6 mg/dL, CSF/serum ratio 0.60). Decreased Abeta42 and Abeta42/40 ratio (0.046) with elevated p-tau181 (84 pg/mL) and total tau (498 pg/mL): amyloid-positive, p-tau-positive biomarker profile of Alzheimer-type pathology. alternatives: Rivastigmine (oral or transdermal patch, fewer gastrointestinal effects with the patch)
interactions: Tamsulosin: no pharmacokinetic interaction; additive risk of dizziness, orthostatic hypotension and syncope with the vagotonic effect of donepezil
Aspirin: cholinesterase inhibitors increase gastric acid secretion; monitor for dyspepsia and gastrointestinal bleeding
Metformin, amlodipine, losartan, rosuvastatin: no clinically relevant interaction
warnings: Vagotonic effect: bradycardia, heart block and syncope; check pulse and ask about syncope before starting (resting heart rate 72 bpm); additive bradycardia if a beta-blocker is added later
Anorexia, nausea and weight loss are common at initiation; record baseline weight given the recent unintentional weight loss
Anticholinergic drugs oppose the effect; avoid co-prescription

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 21/30 with delayed recall 0/3 not improved by category or multiple-choice cues, informant-confirmed decline over two years, and loss of instrumental independence (finances taken over, driving restricted), placing the syndrome at the dementia stage
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive assessment with informant history and functional staging
action_criteria.rationale: Two years of decline reported by his wife must be measured on a validated instrument and staged by whether instrumental independence is lost before it can be attributed [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic profile with severely impaired verbal and visual delayed recall and impaired recognition, plus impaired semantic fluency and naming, with a normal mood screen
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing defines the amnestic multi-domain profile beyond the bedside screen and sets a baseline for tracking [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, electrolytes, hepatic function and inflammatory markers; HbA1c 6.3% on metformin as a vascular risk factor
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, syphilis, HIV and metabolic derangement are treatable contributors and must be screened before the decline is attributed to a neurodegenerative cause [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral medial temporal atrophy (MTA 3 right, 2-3 left) with temporoparietal volume loss disproportionate to age, and only mild-to-moderate small vessel disease (Fazekas 1-2) without infarcts
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with the dementia (volumetric) protocol
action_criteria.rationale: MRI shows the pattern of atrophy and the extent of cerebrovascular disease in a man with diabetes and hypertension, and excludes hydrocephalus and mass lesions [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No contraindicating interaction; tamsulosin adds orthostatic and syncope risk, aspirin gastrointestinal risk, and anorexia may add to his weight loss
action_criteria.label: Check donepezil against the current medicines before starting a cholinesterase inhibitor
action_criteria.rationale: Before a cholinesterase inhibitor is started, his tamsulosin, aspirin and recent weight loss should be reviewed; none contraindicates it, so the check is optional [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the decline to normal aging: he has lost instrumental independence and has an amnestic deficit beyond age norms
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well

Address safety: his confusion on a 30-year route and his wife's restriction of night and unfamiliar driving call for a formal driving evaluation; keep finances with his wife and arrange supervision of medicines and appointments
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines, counseling on dizziness with tamsulosin and recording weight before starting [NICE_NG97]
Evaluate the unintentional weight loss of about five pounds in six months (intake, dentition, mood, age-appropriate screening) and monitor weight during treatment
Manage vascular risk factors: review blood pressure (142/76) toward target if tolerated without orthostatic hypotension, and continue statin and glycemic treatment

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET]

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the dementia work-up; his pulse is regular at 72 and he has no syncope, palpitations or conduction history
Echocardiography does not contribute; there are no infarcts on MRI, no murmur and no heart failure
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; there is no syncope, palpitations or episodic event
Head CT adds nothing when MRI is available and tolerated; MRI is the structural study for the dementia work-up

differential.key_features: No fluctuations, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder or parkinsonism (normal tone, no cogwheeling, normal gait)
No personality change, disinhibition or aggression; quieter but not apathetic out of proportion; naming difficulty without aphasia; temporoparietal and medial temporal rather than frontal atrophy

Diabetes, hypertension and former smoking with Fazekas grade 1-2 white matter changes may contribute, but there are no infarcts or microbleeds and the course is gradual and memory-led with MTA grade 3
Subdued and quieter, but GDS 3/15 and recall not rescued by cues or recognition

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or infectious cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Normal TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, electrolytes and hepatic function; diabetes controlled (HbA1c 6.3%); the unintentional weight loss needs its own evaluation but does not explain a two-year amnestic decline

key_clinical_evidence: Insidious, progressive amnestic decline with impairment in additional domains and loss of instrumental independence meets the NIA-AA 2011 clinical criteria for probable Alzheimer disease dementia; medial temporal atrophy on MRI supports the diagnosis [NIA_AA_2011]
Delayed recall that neither cueing nor recognition rescues indicates a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit, the typical cognitive signature of Alzheimer disease

Mild-to-moderate small vessel disease is common at this age with diabetes and hypertension; it is a contributor to manage and does not displace Alzheimer disease as the primary cause of a memory-led decline
Cholinesterase inhibitors are the first-line symptomatic treatment for mild to moderate Alzheimer dementia; memantine is for moderate or severe disease [NICE_NG97]

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Optional: amyloid status by CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET (one conclusive test), and a donepezil interaction check.
key_educational_points: Early AD typically presents with progressive episodic memory loss as the predominant symptom
Vascular risk factors such as diabetes and hypertension are modifiable contributors to cognitive decline and should be optimized
APOE genotype is a risk modifier and is not a diagnostic test for Alzheimer disease
CSF biomarkers (Abeta42/40, phospho-tau, total tau) or amyloid PET provide in vivo confirmation of Alzheimer pathology; one conclusive test is enough
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line pharmacotherapy for mild-to-moderate AD
Mixed AD and vascular pathology is common and does not preclude an AD diagnosis when the amnestic phenotype predominates

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Takeshi Yamamoto is an 81-year-old right-handed retired city bus driver who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Doris, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties over the past two years. His wife reports that she first noticed changes roughly two years ago when he began misplacing his keys and wallet with increasing frequency, which she initially attributed to normal aging. However, over the past twelve months the problems have become substantially worse and harder to dismiss. He now frequently forgets conversations they had earlier the same day and asks the same questions repeatedly, sometimes three or four times in a single afternoon. He has been an avid fisherman for decades but last summer left his tackle box at the lake on two separate occasions and once drove to a different boat launch than the one he had used for thirty years, becoming confused about which road to take. His wife reports that she discovered unpaid utility bills stuffed in a desk drawer three months ago; he had always handled the household finances meticulously and this was deeply out of character. She has since taken over bill paying and checkbook management. He missed two follow-up appointments with his primary care physician despite having them written on the kitchen calendar, apparently forgetting to check it. At their church, where he has been a deacon for twenty years, fellow members have remarked that he seems quieter than usual and occasionally loses his train of thought during conversations. His wife also notes that he tried to assemble a new bookshelf from a kit two months ago, a task that would have been straightforward for him previously, but became frustrated and confused by the instructions and eventually gave up. He continues to dress, bathe, and feed himself independently, though his wife has begun laying out his clothes because he sometimes picks out mismatched outfits. He still drives locally on familiar routes but his wife no longer feels comfortable with him driving at night or in unfamiliar areas. He denies any hallucinations, personality changes, or aggressive behavior. He has no history of falls, seizures, focal weakness, or tremor. His sleep pattern is unchanged and his wife denies witnessing any acting out of dreams. His appetite is fair, and he has lost approximately five pounds over the past six months without trying. He appears somewhat subdued during the interview and occasionally looks to his wife for confirmation of details but does not appear overtly depressed.
